planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings into rich, shaded, well-drained forest-garden soil in spring; this is one of Fiji's officially recognized noble kava cultivars and needs warmth, humidity, and shelter from direct sun.

directions: Dokobana Vula is one of thirteen kava cultivars officially recognized as 'noble' by Fiji's Ministry of Agriculture, grown mainly on Viti Levu and the eastern islands and typically showing a kavalactone profile associated with gentle, well-balanced effects. Its Fijian name describes the plant itself: 'doko' refers to the thick planting stakes cut from its stems, and 'vula' (pale) describes the light green stem color, which carries numerous raised lenticels along each internode. Grow it as other kava is grown, in shaded, humid conditions with rich, well-drained soil, and expect root harvest only after four or more years, since Fiji's export standard ties noble-grade quality to that minimum age. Avoid open sun or soggy ground, both of which stunt growth and invite root rot in this slow-maturing shrub.
sources: Fiji Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji Kava (Yaqona) Standard 2017
PHAMA Plus, 'Development of a Yaqona Quality Manual: Survey of Varieties of Yaqona Grown in Fiji'
Kavalactone Content and Profile of Kava Cultivated on Taveuni, Qamea, and Rabi Islands of Fiji, Agriculture (MDPI), 2025

common_name: Loa Kasa Balavu Kava (Fijian Noble Yaqona)

planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings into rich, shaded, well-drained garden soil in spring; distinguished by dark purple stems with long internodes among Fiji's noble kava cultivars.

directions: Loa Kasa Balavu is a traditional Fijian noble kava cultivar distinguished by dark purple stems with long, thin internodes, in contrast to its shorter-jointed sibling cultivar Loa Kasa Leka. It is commonly reported among the noble cultivars with a calmer, less stimulating kavalactone profile favored for everyday ceremonial and social drinking in Fiji. Propagate and grow it exactly as other kava, from stem cuttings set into shaded, humid, well-drained soil, and plan on a minimum of four years of growth before harvesting roots for noble-grade quality. Because it is a sterile cultivar maintained only by vegetative propagation, source clean planting material to avoid spreading soilborne disease between gardens.
sources: Fiji Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji Kava (Yaqona) Standard 2017
PHAMA Plus, 'Development of a Yaqona Quality Manual: Survey of Varieties of Yaqona Grown in Fiji'
Kavalactone Content and Profile of Kava Cultivated on Taveuni, Qamea, and Rabi Islands of Fiji, Agriculture (MDPI), 2025

common_name: Vula Kasa Leka Kava (Fijian Noble Yaqona)

planting.note: Set rooted stem cuttings into rich, shaded, well-drained garden soil in spring; a short-internode, pale-stemmed Fijian noble kava cultivar.

directions: Vula Kasa Leka is a short-internode, pale-stemmed Fijian noble kava cultivar whose name translates roughly as 'short pale stem,' distinguishing it from the longer-jointed Vula Kasa Balavu. Chemical surveys of Fiji's kava crop have repeatedly placed it among the cultivars with a kavalactone profile generally linked to mild, sociable effects rather than strong sedation. Like all kava, it must be grown from cuttings in warm, humid, deeply shaded garden conditions with loose, fertile, well-drained soil, since direct sun and waterlogging both check its growth badly. Fiji's own quality standard treats root age as the main marker of quality, so let plants grow undisturbed for at least four years before lifting any roots.
sources: Fiji Ministry of Agriculture, Fiji Kava (Yaqona) Standard 2017
PHAMA Plus, 'Development of a Yaqona Quality Manual: Survey of Varieties of Yaqona Grown in Fiji'
Kavalactone Content and Profile of Kava Cultivated on Taveuni, Qamea, and Rabi Islands of Fiji, Agriculture (MDPI), 2025

planting.note: Set huli (corm-top cuttings) into rich, consistently moist soil once soil has warmed; bred at USP Alafua in Samoa for better drought and low-fertility performance than traditional cultivars.

directions: Alafua Sunrise is a named taro cultivar released from the breeding program at the University of the South Pacific's Alafua campus in Samoa, selected from a sexually propagated seedling population rather than from a traditional clonal landrace. In regional yield trials it outproduced the long-standing local cultivar 'Niue' by roughly 13 to 50 percent, with its biggest advantage showing up on drought-prone or nutrient-poor ground, and it also showed fewer dasheen mosaic virus symptoms than older cultivars. Its corms have yellow flesh that some local cooks consider less visually appealing than whiter traditional types, but its vigorous early growth and strong sucker production make it dependable for home and market gardens. Grow it exactly as other upland dalo, in rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade, and expect corms to size up over roughly nine to eleven months.
sources: Ivancic, A. et al., 'Alafua Sunrise and Samoa Hybrid Improve the Production of Taro (Colocasia esculenta [L] Schott) in the Pacific', Acta Horticulturae 380
Crop Profile for Taro in American Samoa (USDA/IPM Centers, 1999)

planting.note: Set huli (corm-top cuttings) into rich, consistently moist soil once soil has warmed; bred at USP Alafua in Samoa and notably tolerant of both wet and well-drained ground.

directions: Samoa Hybrid was released alongside Alafua Sunrise as one of the first two improved, breeding-program-derived taro cultivars developed at the University of the South Pacific's Alafua campus in Samoa, rather than being a traditional selected clone. Trials found it produced roughly 50 percent more fresh corm weight than older traditional cultivars while performing equally well in both well-drained and poorly drained soils, along with noticeably better plant vigor and sucker production. Because it tolerates a wider range of soil drainage than most dalo, it suits growers whose plots include both low, wetter ground and better-drained rises. Set out huli into fertile, consistently moist soil in partial shade, and plan on roughly nine to eleven months to full corm maturity.
sources: Ivancic, A. et al., 'Alafua Sunrise and Samoa Hybrid Improve the Production of Taro (Colocasia esculenta [L] Schott) in the Pacific', Acta Horticulturae 380
Crop Profile for Taro in American Samoa (USDA/IPM Centers, 1999)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or tissue-cultured tree in spring in rich, deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Puou is an old, widely distributed Pacific breadfruit valued for its productivity and quick cooking.

directions: Puou is an old, widely grown breadfruit cultivar documented across Samoa, Tonga, Fiji, the Cook Islands, and Vanuatu, and considered by Samoan growers to be among the best-tasting varieties available. Its fruit is variably spherical, ovoid, or heart-shaped, averaging around 17 by 16 centimeters and roughly 1.7 kilograms, with an irregularly bumpy, flattened-pebble skin covering pale to light yellow flesh around a modest number of seeds. The tree is a reliable, relatively low, early producer that sends up numerous root suckers and whose fruit is reported to cook quickly, both useful traits for home orchards and small farms. Grow it like other named breadfruit varieties in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, sheltered from strong wind and any temperatures below the mid-50s Fahrenheit, and expect first fruit within a few years of planting.
sources: Breadfruit Institute, National Tropical Botanical Garden, Breadfruit Variety Database (entry: 'Puou')
Ragone, D., 'Breadfruit Varieties in the Pacific' (Artocarpus altilis germplasm collection)

planting.note: Plant a pup or potted division after frost danger passes; a Fe'i-type landrace from Samoa's Manu'a Islands with upright-bearing fruit bunches.

directions: Soa'a is a Fe'i-type banana landrace documented on Samoa's Manu'a Islands, where it was historically grown on royal plantation land and, unlike most other Samoan bananas, apparently never spread to the main islands of Samoa. Collecting surveys describe its fruit as somewhat elongated with a short pedicel and its leaves as more lax and horizontal than those of the related cultivar Ausulasula, and its flesh cooks to a dense, deep orange color valued for boiling, baking, or cooking in an underground umu oven. Like other Fe'i bananas, the plant carries its fruit bunch upright rather than hanging, a trait that sets the whole group apart from ordinary dessert and cooking bananas at a glance. Give it the same culture as other large tropical bananas: deep, fertile, constantly moist soil, full sun, and shelter from wind, since it is strictly tropical and intolerant of any cold.
sources: Sachter-Smith, G. & Sardos, J., 'Bananas of Samoa' (Bioversity International/CGIAR, Samoa banana collecting mission catalog, SAM006/SAM013)

planting.note: Plant a pup or potted division after frost danger passes; a Fe'i-type landrace from Samoa's outer islands with upright-bearing fruit bunches and very erect leaves.

directions: Ausulasula is a Fe'i-type Samoan banana landrace documented alongside the related cultivar Soa'a during banana-diversity collecting surveys, distinguished in the field by fruit that is somewhat rounder with a distinctly longer pedicel and by leaves that stand very erect rather than lax. As with other Fe'i bananas, its fruit bunch grows upright above the crown of leaves instead of drooping, and the starchy flesh is typically boiled, baked, or roasted rather than eaten raw. It persists as a traditional dooryard and plantation planting on Samoa's outer islands rather than as a commercial export type, grown more for subsistence and ceremonial use than for market sale. Cultivate it like other large tropical bananas, in deep, moisture-retentive, fertile soil in full sun with good wind shelter, since it has no cold tolerance and needs consistently warm, humid conditions to thrive.
sources: Sachter-Smith, G. & Sardos, J., 'Bananas of Samoa' (Bioversity International/CGIAR, Samoa banana collecting mission catalog, SAM001/SAM005)
